q: Federal law should preempt all state AI regulation so that companies face one national rulebook.
r: States should keep the power to regulate AI even where this produces multiple rulebooks companies must follow.
p: One national AI rulebook, with state laws wiped out, is the right structure.

q: Binding AI regulation should be enacted now on the best available evidence, accepting that some rules will later prove mistaken.
r: Binding AI regulation should wait for better evidence, accepting that some harms will occur in the meantime.
p: Legislate now and fix mistakes later, rather than wait for certainty while harms accrue.

q: The EU's decision to delay high-risk AI compliance deadlines by over a year was right, because the original rules were unworkable.
r: The EU's decision to delay high-risk AI compliance deadlines by over a year was wrong, because it rewarded industry pressure.
p: Pushing back the EU's high-risk deadlines was the correct call given how unworkable the rules were.

q: Frontier AI developers should need a government license to operate, as banks and nuclear operators do.
r: Frontier AI developers should not need a government license to operate.
p: Running a frontier lab should require a license, like running a bank or a reactor.

q: Regulatory sandboxes that exempt AI firms from rules while they experiment do more good than harm.
r: Regulatory sandboxes that exempt AI firms from rules while they experiment do more harm than good.
p: Letting firms test outside the rules in a sandbox is a net win.

q: AI liability rules should presume the developer is at fault when a high-risk system causes harm, shifting the burden of proof to the developer.
r: AI liability rules should require the injured party to prove developer fault when a high-risk system causes harm.
x: burden of proof in AI liability
p: When a high-risk AI hurts someone, the developer should have to prove it was not their fault.

q: Sector regulators applying existing law to AI will produce better outcomes than a dedicated AI regulator.
r: A dedicated AI regulator will produce better outcomes than sector regulators applying existing law.
p: Let the finance, health, and consumer regulators handle AI; do not build an AI agency.

q: Companies deploying AI in hiring should be required to publish annual independent bias audits, as some cities already require.
r: Companies deploying AI in hiring should not be required to publish annual independent bias audits.
p: Yearly independent bias audits should be compulsory for hiring AI.

q: A state that repeals a broad AI act in favor of a narrower disclosure law has improved its regulation.
r: A state that repeals a broad AI act in favor of a narrower disclosure law has weakened its regulation.
x: comprehensive versus narrow state AI law
p: Swapping a sweeping AI statute for a slim disclosure law is a step forward.

q: Any AI system used to make decisions affecting more than 100,000 people per year should be registered in a public algorithm register.
r: AI systems used to make decisions affecting more than 100,000 people per year should not have to be registered in a public register.
p: Systems deciding for a hundred thousand people a year belong on a public register.

q: Voluntary AI safety standards backed by procurement preferences will achieve more than mandatory rules.
r: Mandatory rules will achieve more than voluntary AI safety standards backed by procurement preferences.
p: Voluntary standards with procurement carrots beat binding mandates.

q: Mandatory independent third-party safety audits should be required for every frontier model before deployment in a jurisdiction.
r: Independent third-party safety audits should not be mandatory for frontier model deployment.
p: No independent audit, no deployment, for every frontier model.

q: Frontier AI rules should apply only to developers above $500 million in annual revenue, exempting everyone smaller.
r: Frontier AI rules should apply based on model capability, not developer revenue, with no exemption for smaller developers.
p: Only companies making half a billion a year should face frontier AI rules.

q: AI companies should be barred from lobbying on AI safety legislation while they hold government evaluation contracts.
r: AI companies should be free to lobby on AI safety legislation while holding government evaluation contracts.
p: A lab under government contract to be evaluated should not be lobbying on the rules.

q: AI-specific legislation is unnecessary; existing consumer protection, tort, and criminal law cover every real AI harm.
r: AI-specific legislation is necessary; existing consumer protection, tort, and criminal law leave real AI harms uncovered.
p: We do not need AI laws; the laws we have already reach every genuine AI harm.

q: Whistleblower protections specific to AI safety concerns should be enacted, covering employees who report to regulators or the public.
r: AI-specific whistleblower protections are unnecessary; general employment law suffices.
p: AI safety whistleblowers need their own legal shield.

q: Rules requiring human review of every automated decision produce rubber-stamping and should be replaced with outcome audits.
r: Rules requiring human review of every automated decision should be kept rather than replaced with outcome audits.
p: Mandatory human sign-off just gets rubber-stamped; audit outcomes instead.

q: Developers should be required to disclose training data sources in enough detail for rights holders to check whether their works were used.
r: Developers should not be required to disclose training data sources in detail sufficient for rights holders to check for their works.
p: Training data should be disclosed well enough that a creator can find out if their work is in it.

q: Legislatures should write AI law in technology-neutral terms and leave definitions of 'frontier' or 'high-risk' to regulators.
r: Legislatures should write specific definitions of 'frontier' and 'high-risk' into AI law rather than delegating them to regulators.
p: Keep statutes general and let agencies define the technical lines.

q: Companies should be required to notify affected people whenever an AI system makes a consequential decision about them, with a right to human appeal.
r: Companies should not be required to notify people of consequential AI decisions or to offer human appeal.
p: If an AI decides something important about you, you should be told and be able to appeal to a person.

q: Innovation-first AI laws like Japan's, which emphasize promotion over restriction, are a better model than the EU's risk-based approach.
r: The EU's risk-based approach is a better model than innovation-first AI laws like Japan's.
p: Japan's promote-first AI law is a better template than Europe's risk tiers.

q: Penalties for violating frontier AI safety rules should scale to at least 5% of global annual revenue.
r: Penalties for violating frontier AI safety rules should be capped well below 5% of global annual revenue.
p: Breaking frontier safety rules should cost at least five percent of worldwide revenue.

q: State laws requiring chatbots to disclose they are not human are unnecessary because users already assume this.
r: State laws requiring chatbots to disclose they are not human are necessary because many users do not assume this.
p: Nobody needs a law telling them the chatbot is a bot.

q: Governments should ban AI systems designed to provide mental health therapy without a licensed clinician in the loop.
r: Governments should permit AI systems that provide mental health therapy with no licensed clinician in the loop.
p: AI therapy with no licensed human involved should be illegal.

q: A national AI law should include a broad safe harbor for developers who follow recognized voluntary standards.
r: A national AI law should not include a safe harbor for developers who follow voluntary standards.
p: Following recognized voluntary standards should shield developers from liability.

q: AI regulation should include sunset clauses forcing every rule to be re-enacted within five years or expire.
r: AI regulation should not include sunset clauses; rules should persist until repealed.
p: Every AI rule should expire after five years unless renewed.

q: Private litigation, not agency enforcement, should be the main mechanism for holding AI companies accountable for harm.
r: Agency enforcement, not private litigation, should be the main mechanism for holding AI companies accountable for harm.
p: Lawsuits, not regulators, should be the main check on AI companies.

q: Developers of general-purpose models should be required to publish a public summary of copyrighted content used in training, as EU law requires.
r: Developers of general-purpose models should not be required to publish summaries of copyrighted training content.
p: A public summary of what copyrighted material trained the model should be mandatory.

q: Laws that let people opt out of automated decision-making do more harm than good because they slow services for everyone.
r: Laws that let people opt out of automated decision-making do more good than harm despite slowing services.
p: Opt-out rights for automated decisions gum up services and are not worth it.

q: Regulators should be given the power to demand model access and run their own tests on any AI system deployed in their jurisdiction.
r: Regulators should not have power to demand model access and run their own tests on deployed AI systems.
p: Any regulator should be able to get the model and test it themselves.

q: Cities should not regulate AI at all; the issues are too complex for local government.
r: Cities should regulate AI in areas like policing and public services, despite the complexity.
p: AI regulation is beyond city hall; leave it to higher levels.

q: Any AI law should require developers to maintain an incident database open to researchers, not just to regulators.
r: AI incident databases should be available to regulators only, not to researchers.
p: Incident records should be open to researchers, not locked with regulators.

q: The greater regulatory risk today is over-regulation stifling beneficial AI, not under-regulation permitting harm.
r: The greater regulatory risk today is under-regulation permitting harm, not over-regulation stifling beneficial AI.
p: Right now, too much AI regulation is the bigger danger than too little.

q: Developers should be legally required to keep a pre-release model in escrow with a regulator so it can be examined after any incident.
r: Developers should not be required to keep pre-release models in escrow with a regulator.
p: A copy of each model should sit in regulator escrow for post-incident examination.

q: A 269-page comprehensive federal AI bill is the wrong approach; narrow, single-issue statutes would work better.
r: A comprehensive federal AI bill is the right approach; narrow, single-issue statutes would leave gaps.
p: Skip the omnibus AI bill; pass small, targeted laws instead.
